constraints: b != m1 and b != m2 and b != m3 and b != m4
solution: Write down the factors. The first coefficient ${=a}$ has the factor pairs $1\times{=a}$ and ${=p}\times{=p}$. The constant term ${=c}$ has the factor pairs $1\times{=c}$ and ${=q}\times{=q}$.

Every term of ${=a}x^{2}+{=b}x+{=c}$ is positive, so every bracket contains a plus sign. Set out the possible pairs of brackets from the factor pairs: $(x+1)({=a}x+{=c})$, $(x+{=c})({=a}x+1)$, $(x+{=q})({=a}x+{=q})$, $({=p}x+1)({=p}x+{=c})$ and $({=p}x+{=q})({=p}x+{=q})$.

The trinomial has middle term ${=b}x$, and only the last pair of brackets gives this. Here the first term and the last term are both perfect squares and the two brackets are identical: ${=a}x^{2}+{=b}x+{=c}=({=p}x+{=q})({=p}x+{=q})$.

Check by multiplying out. The first terms give ${=p}x\times{=p}x={=a}x^{2}$, the last terms give ${=q}\times{=q}={=c}$, and the middle term is $({=p}\times{=q}+{=q}\times{=p})x=({=p*q}+{=p*q})x={=b}x$. This is the original trinomial, so the factorisation is correct.
notes: The twist the book itself uses in ex1-11-29g (16b^2+56b+49 = (4b+7)(4b+7)): a perfect-square trinomial, where the two brackets are identical. Here a = p^2 and c = q^2 with p, q distinct primes from 2, 3, 5, 7, so each of a and c has exactly two factor pairs (1 x n and root x root) and there are exactly five candidate bracket pairs, all listed and expanded; their middle terms are pairwise different from the correct 2pq (checked over the whole parameter space, constraint included). gcd(p, q) = 1 keeps the trinomial primitive. The book's own example has a composite root (4), which is left out on purpose so that every factor-pair list in the solution is complete. The marker answer is the repeated product, as in the book's key; if the form check rejects a power, (px+q)^2 is the same answer. Every equation in every rendered solution was checked by evaluation over the whole parameter space (12 instances).
